title: Badge Subsets
statement: A hackathon awards a set of distinct badge numbers, and a team can display any selection of them, including none. List every possible selection. Write each selection in increasing order, and order the list by selection size first, then lexicographically by number (compare the first numbers, then the second, and so on).

hints.content: Each badge is either in a selection or not, so there are 2^n selections.
Sorting the badges first makes it easier to produce each selection in increasing order.
For a fixed size k, choosing positions in increasing order produces the k-selections lexicographically.
Backtrack: pick the next badge from positions after the last one picked, recurse until k are picked, then undo the pick.
Run that for k = 0, 1, ..., n to get the required overall order without a final sort.

testCases.explanation: Input order does not affect the output order.

solutions.title: Bitmask enumeration and sort
solutions.intuition: Each integer from 0 to 2^n - 1 is a membership pattern.
solutions.approach: For every mask, collect badges whose bit is set and sort them. Sort the list of selections by length, then element by element.
solutions.pseudocode:
for mask in 0 .. 2^n - 1: out.push(sorted badges with bit set)
sort out by (length, elements)
commonMistakes: Comparing selections with default string sorting, which puts [10] before [2].
solutions.interviewExplanation: Bitmasks enumerate every subset cleanly. The required order then needs a custom comparator and a full sort of 2^n lists.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Sorting by size, then lexicographically, gives the required list.

solutions.title: Backtracking by size
solutions.intuition: Choosing increasing positions from a sorted array produces combinations in lexicographic order, so looping over sizes yields the exact output order.
solutions.approach: Sort the badges. For each size k, run choose(start, picked): if k are picked, record a copy; otherwise try each index from start up to the last index that still leaves room, push it, recurse with i + 1, then pop.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort badges
for k in 0..n: choose(0, [])
choose(start, picked): if |picked| == k: record; return
  for i in start .. n - (k - |picked|): push b[i]; choose(i+1, picked); pop
commonMistakes: Pushing picked itself instead of a copy, so every recorded selection ends up empty.
Forgetting to pop after recursing, which corrupts later selections.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Each output selection takes O(n) to copy and there are 2^n of them, so O(2^n · n) is optimal for producing the list. I sort once, then for each size run a standard combinations backtrack with increasing indices, which emits each size's selections in lexicographic order. The bound i <= n - (k - picked) prunes branches that can't reach k.
